title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: a teacher's hand curled closed, a student's promises, and the book that came of one of them

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Alvar hymns: ten verses that led Nathamuni to a thousand, and a lost Tamil Veda handed back, through a line of teachers that would reach Ramanuja.
screen: `THE TAMIL VEDA, FOUND AGAIN.` · `TODAY: RAMANUJA'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: A hand, curled closed. The Sri Vaishnava tradition says that when the young Ramanuja hurried to meet the great teacher Yamuna, he arrived too late. Yamuna had died, and some fingers of his hand were curled tight, as if holding on to something. Those around him read them as wishes left undone. Ramanuja stood by the body and made promises aloud, and with each one, the story says, a finger straightened. One of those promises was a book: the Sri Bhashya.
screen: `A HAND, CURLED CLOSED.` → `A PROMISE FOR EACH FINGER.` → `ONE OF THEM WAS A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The promise was a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and the student kept it. The Brahma Sutras are tiny, packed lines, too short to understand alone. A bhashya is a commentary that opens them up, line by line. And the Sri Bhashya argues in the open. Again and again Ramanuja sets out the opposing view first, in full, as if a sharp rival were sitting across from him, and only then answers. Indian commentaries call that the purvapaksha, the prior view. Among his opponents are other Vedanta teachers, and he gives their arguments at length before replying. What does he argue for? That the Brahman of the Upanishads is a person, Narayana, Vishnu, full of every good quality and free of every fault. That the world is real. That each self is real, and never apart from God. And that the Upanishads, the Gita and the Alvars' devotion are saying one thing, not several. Theology, in this book, means thinking hard about a God you can also love. Over the next days, a few of its pieces, one at a time.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A TEACHER'S HAND.` · `BHASHYA: OPENING A TINY LINE.` · `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `A GOD TO THINK ABOUT, AND LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one disagreement you're carrying, at home or at work; small is fine. In your head, say the other person's side as well as you can, in full, as if you were defending it, and stay there a few breaths before your own view comes back. Notice whether anything shifts; if you pray, rest in the name you pray to as you sit with both.
Vaishnava theology. Today, Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya: a promise to a teacher, a commentary that states the other view first, and a God to think about and love.
Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). A promise at a teacher's side became a book that hears the other side first. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, the Sri Bhashya is studied with a teacher, often alongside its later commentaries, and students learn its method: set out the opposing view in full, then answer it from the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja, standing by your teacher's body, some of his fingers curled closed. what do you do?
options: leave quietly; it's too late now.
promise aloud to finish what he hoped for.
start a school of your own and forget the rest.
fork.reveal: the story says Ramanuja made promises aloud, one of them a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and with each one a finger straightened.

original.note: Sanskrit: Ramanuja's commentary on the Brahma Sutras, the core text of Sri Vaishnava theology.

trapdoor: what you thought: theology is dry rules about God.
what it means: in the Sri Bhashya, it's hard, open argument about a God who can also be loved.
what a scholar hears: a bhashya on the Brahma Sutras in purvapaksha and siddhanta form, arguing Vishishtadvaita against rival Vedanta readings.
recall: the ultimate reality, ground of all

chat.says: Ramanuja's big book spends pages on his opponents' views. Isn't that a strange way to argue?
options: It's his method: he sets out the other view first, in full, then answers it.
He quotes rivals only briefly, to show how weak their arguments are.
He lists every school's view equally and never argues for his own.
chat.meaning: The Sri Bhashya states the purvapaksha, the prior view, in full before replying, and then argues for its own reading.

Yamuna.meaning: the great teacher Ramanuja arrived too late to meet

Sri Bhashya.meaning: Ramanuja's commentary on the Brahma Sutras

Brahma Sutras.meaning: tiny, packed lines summing up the Upanishads' teaching

purvapaksha.meaning: the prior view: the opponent's case, set out first

Narayana.meaning: a name of Vishnu, the person Ramanuja calls Brahman

sources.ref: Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya (method: purvapaksha and siddhanta; Brahman as the Supreme Person with good qualities)

notes: Editor: the writer's hook told the Tirukoshtiyur temple-tower story, already told in year one (day 289) and recalled on day 290; the hook now opens on Yamuna's curled fingers (moved up from the teach), and the fork and a match pair no longer use the tower. The review now picks up the re-angled day 1225 (Nathamuni and the ten verses). 'His rivals are other Vedanta teachers' became 'among his opponents' (the Sri Bhashya also answers non-Vedanta schools); 'in its strongest form' became 'in full'.
The curled-fingers story is told as tradition; the number of fingers and the other promises are deliberately left out ('some fingers', 'one of those promises').
Thibaut's 1904 English translation of the Sri Bhashya (Sacred Books of the East 48) exists but is not on the public-domain list the validator knows, so nothing is quoted.

The summary of the Sri Bhashya's claims (Brahman as Narayana with all good qualities and no faults; the world and selves real and inseparable; the scriptures in harmony) should be checked by a Sri Vaishnava Keeper.
